lessons.title: Direct Seeding vs. Transplanting
lessons.body:
When planting onions, you have two main choices: direct seeding or transplanting. Direct seeding means sowing seeds straight into the field where the onions will grow. Transplanting means starting seeds in a nursery bed or seedbed, then moving the young seedlings to the field later. Each method has pros and cons, and your choice depends on your land, labour, and water supply.

Direct seeding is faster and less labour-intensive. You sow seeds directly into prepared soil, spacing them about 1 cm apart in rows 30 cm apart. But onions from direct seeding need very fine, weed-free soil and consistent moisture. Seeds are small and weak; they can be washed away by heavy rain or choked by weeds. Also, you need more seedâabout 4-5 kg per hectareâbecause not all will germinate. Direct seeding works best in large fields with good irrigation and where labour is scarce.

Transplanting gives you more control. You raise seedlings in a nursery bed for 4-6 weeks, then move them to the field. This lets you start early, protect seedlings from harsh weather, and select only strong plants. You use less seedâabout 2-3 kg per hectareâand you can prepare the main field while seedlings grow. Transplanting also allows you to space plants precisely, which leads to uniform bulbs. However, it requires more labour: preparing nursery beds, watering, pulling seedlings, and replanting. The shock of transplanting can slow growth if not done carefully.

In Africa, many smallholder farmers prefer transplanting because it gives better control over water and weeds, especially in areas with erratic rainfall. But if you have a large farm, good irrigation, and limited labour, direct seeding can save time and money. Whichever you choose, ensure your soil is loose, fertile, and well-drained. Onions hate compacted soil and waterlogging. Test your choice on a small plot first to see what works best on your farm.

lessons.title: Starting Onions from Seed Indoors
lessons.body:
Starting onions indoors gives you a head start, especially if your rainy season is short or your field is not ready. You can use seed trays, wooden boxes, or even old plastic containers. The goal is to produce strong, healthy seedlings that are ready to transplant in 4-6 weeks.

First, prepare your seed-starting mix. Use a light, well-draining medium: mix equal parts of river sand, compost, and garden soil. Sterilize the soil if possible by pouring boiling water over it and letting it coolâthis kills weed seeds and diseases. Fill your trays or boxes with this mix, leaving about 2 cm at the top. Water the mix thoroughly before sowing.

Sow seeds thinlyâabout 1 cm apartâand cover with a thin layer of sand or fine soil, no more than 0.5 cm deep. Onion seeds need light to germinate, so don't bury them deep. Water gently with a fine spray to avoid washing seeds away. Cover the trays with a plastic sheet or a light cloth to keep moisture in. Keep the trays in a warm, sunny spot, but protect them from heavy rain. Ideal temperature for germination is 20-25Â°C. Seeds should sprout in 7-14 days.

Once seedlings emerge, remove the cover and place them where they get at least 6 hours of sunlight daily. Water regularly but not excessivelyâkeep the soil moist, not soggy. If seedlings are too crowded, thin them to 2-3 cm apart to prevent weak, spindly growth. You can feed them with a weak liquid fertilizer (like diluted chicken manure tea) every two weeks. Avoid high-nitrogen fertilizers, which encourage leafy growth instead of strong roots.

Hardening off is crucial before transplanting. About a week before you move them to the field, reduce watering and expose seedlings to more sun and wind gradually. This toughens them up. By 4-6 weeks, seedlings should be pencil-thick and 10-15 cm tall. Then they are ready for the field. Starting indoors gives you healthier plants and a earlier harvest.

lessons.title: Transplanting Seedlings to the Field
lessons.body:
Transplanting is a critical stepâif done poorly, seedlings can die or grow slowly. The best time to transplant is late afternoon or on a cloudy day, so the sun doesn't scorch the young plants. Water the nursery bed thoroughly a few hours before lifting seedlings. This makes it easier to pull them without damaging roots.

Prepare your field at least two weeks before transplanting. Dig the soil to a depth of 20-30 cm, remove weeds and stones, and mix in well-rotted manure or compost (about 2-3 wheelbarrows per 100 square meters). Make raised beds 1 meter wide and 20 cm high if your area gets heavy rain; this improves drainage. Onions hate waterlogged roots. If your soil is acidic, add a little wood ash or lime.

When lifting seedlings, use a small fork or stick to loosen the soil around them. Hold the seedling by the leaf, not the stem, and gently pull. Try to keep a small ball of soil around the roots. If roots are long, trim them to about 2-3 cm with a sharp knifeâthis encourages new root growth. Sort seedlings: discard any with damaged roots, thick necks, or disease. Only plant the best.

Make holes in the field with a dibber (a pointed stick) or your finger, about 2-3 cm deep. Space holes 10-15 cm apart in rows 20-30 cm apart. Place one seedling per hole, with the roots spread out. Firm the soil around the roots gently but firmlyâno air pockets. After planting, water each seedling immediately. Keep the soil moist for the first week. If the sun is strong, provide temporary shade using palm fronds or shade net for 2-3 days.

Transplanting shock can set plants back. To reduce it, avoid planting in hot midday sun, keep roots moist, and water daily until new growth appears. Within a week, you should see new leaves. Then you can reduce watering to twice a week. Proper transplanting gives you uniform stands and better bulb development.

lessons.title: Using Sets and Bulbs for Planting
lessons.body:
Onions can also be grown from sets (small bulbs) or from mature bulbs. This method is faster than seed, but it has trade-offs. Sets are small onion bulbs, about 1-2 cm in diameter, grown from seed the previous year. They are planted directly into the field and produce mature bulbs in 60-90 days, much quicker than seed (which takes 100-120 days).

To plant sets, prepare your field as for transplanting: loose, fertile, well-drained soil. Plant sets 2-3 cm deep, pointed end up, spaced 10-15 cm apart in rows 20-30 cm apart. Cover with soil and firm gently. Water immediately. Sets are easy to handle and rarely fail, but they are more expensive than seed. Also, if sets are not stored properly, they can bolt (produce flower stalks) instead of forming bulbs. To avoid bolting, choose sets smaller than 2 cm and plant them in cool weather, not during extreme heat.

Planting mature bulbs is less common but possible. You can plant small bulbs from the previous harvest. However, large bulbs tend to bolt and produce seeds rather than a good bulb. If you use bulbs, choose ones that are 2-3 cm across and plant them the same way as sets. They will produce green onions (spring onions) if harvested early, or bulbs if left longer. But bulb-to-bulb planting is not recommended for large-scale production because it's costly and yields are lower.

In Africa, sets are popular in urban gardens and for off-season production because they are quick and reliable. But for commercial farming, seed is more economical. If you use sets, buy certified disease-free sets from a reputable supplier. Never plant sets that are soft, mouldy, or sprouting. Rotate crops: don't plant onions after onions or after garlic, as pests and diseases build up in the soil. Sets and bulbs can be a useful tool in your onion farming, but use them wisely.

lessons.title: Spacing and Plant Density
lessons.body:
Spacing determines how much space each onion plant has to grow. If plants are too close, they compete for water, nutrients, and sunlight, resulting in small bulbs. If too far apart, you waste land and get lower yields per hectare. The ideal spacing for onions depends on the variety, soil fertility, and market preference.

For bulb onions, the recommended spacing is 10-15 cm between plants and 20-30 cm between rows. This gives a plant density of about 30-40 plants per square meter. In Africa, many farmers use 10 cm x 20 cm, which is about 50 plants per square meter. But on poor soil, wider spacing (15 cm x 30 cm) is better because each plant needs more area to find nutrients. On fertile soil, closer spacing can be used. The goal is to maximize yield without sacrificing bulb size.

For green onions (spring onions), you can plant closer: 5-7 cm between plants and 15-20 cm between rows. This gives higher plant density and more stems per area. For sets, spacing is similar to transplants: 10-15 cm x 20-30 cm. If you are growing for pickling onions (small bulbs), you can plant at 5 cm x 15 cm to get many small bulbs.

To achieve correct spacing, use a measuring stick or a marked rope. Make furrows or holes at the right distance. Don't guessâmeasure. After planting, you can mulch between rows to suppress weeds and conserve moisture. Remember that onions have shallow roots, so they don't compete well with weeds. Proper spacing makes weeding easier.

Plant density also affects airflow, which influences disease. Too dense, and fungal diseases like downy mildew spread quickly. Too sparse, and you lose yield. Aim for a uniform stand. If gaps occur, replant with spare seedlings. Consistent spacing leads to uniform bulb size, which fetches better prices at market. So take time to space correctly.

lessons.title: Timing Planting for Optimal Bulbing
lessons.body:
Onions are day-length sensitive. Bulbingâthe process where the plant stops making leaves and starts swelling the bulbâis triggered by the length of daylight. Each variety has a critical day length: short-day varieties bulb when days are 10-12 hours, long-day varieties need 14-16 hours. In Africa, most regions near the equator have 12 hours of daylight year-round, so short-day varieties are best. But if you plant at the wrong time, you may get lots of leaves and no bulbs.

Timing planting is crucial. For short-day onions in tropical Africa, plant at the start of the cool dry season, when temperatures are moderate and days are shortening or stable. For example, in Kenya, plant in March-April for harvest in August-September. In Nigeria, plant in October-November for harvest in February-March. Avoid planting in the hottest months, as high temperatures (above 30Â°C) can cause bolting or poor bulb formation. Also, avoid planting too late: if bulbs start forming when days are still long, they may not size up properly.

In areas with distinct rainy and dry seasons, plant onions at the beginning of the dry season, using irrigation. If you plant during heavy rains, you risk root rot and fungal diseases. Also, onions need about 100-120 days from seed to harvest (or 60-90 days from sets). Count backwards from your target harvest date to determine planting time. For example, if you want to harvest in December, plant seeds in August-September.

Soil temperature also matters. Onion seeds germinate best when soil is 15-25Â°C. If soil is too hot, germination is poor. You can start seeds in a nursery and transplant when conditions are better. For sets, plant when soil is at least 10Â°C. In cooler highland areas, plant in early spring to take advantage of longer days. Always check with local extension officers for the best planting calendar for your area. Proper timing ensures good bulbing and high yields.

quiz.q: What is the main advantage of transplanting onions over direct seeding?
options: C) It gives better control over spacing and water
quiz.explanation: Transplanting allows precise spacing and better water management, leading to uniform bulbs.

quiz.q: How much seed is needed per hectare for direct seeding of onions?
quiz.explanation: Direct seeding requires 4-5 kg of seed per hectare due to lower germination and weed competition.

quiz.q: Which method is preferred by many smallholder farmers in Africa?
quiz.explanation: Transplanting gives better control over water and weeds, which is crucial in areas with erratic rainfall.

quiz.q: What is the ideal depth to sow onion seeds indoors?
quiz.explanation: Onion seeds need light to germinate, so they should be covered with only a thin layer of soil, about 0.5 cm.

quiz.q: How long does it take for onion seedlings to be ready for transplanting?
quiz.explanation: Seedlings are typically ready for transplanting 4-6 weeks after sowing when they are pencil-thick.

quiz.q: What is hardening off?
options: B) Gradually exposing seedlings to outdoor conditions
D) Cutting the roots of seedlings
quiz.explanation: Hardening off is the process of gradually acclimating seedlings to sun, wind, and cooler temperatures before transplanting.

quiz.q: When is the best time of day to transplant onion seedlings?
options: C) Late afternoon or cloudy day
quiz.explanation: Late afternoon or cloudy conditions reduce transplanting shock and sun scorch.

quiz.q: Why should you trim the roots of onion seedlings before transplanting?
options: A) To make them easier to plant
B) To encourage new root growth
quiz.explanation: Trimming roots to 2-3 cm stimulates the growth of new feeder roots.

quiz.q: What is the recommended spacing for bulb onions?
quiz.explanation: 10-15 cm between plants and 20-30 cm between rows is ideal for bulb onions.

quiz.q: What is a set in onion farming?
options: B) A small bulb grown from seed
quiz.explanation: Sets are small onion bulbs, about 1-2 cm in diameter, grown from seed the previous year.

quiz.q: Why is it important to avoid planting large bulbs for bulb production?
options: B) They tend to bolt and produce seeds
quiz.explanation: Large bulbs are more likely to bolt (produce flower stalks) instead of forming a good bulb.

quiz.q: What is bolting in onions?
quiz.explanation: Bolting is when the onion plant sends up a flower stalk, which reduces bulb quality.

quiz.q: How many plants per square meter are recommended for bulb onions?
quiz.explanation: A density of 30-40 plants per square meter is typical for bulb onions.

quiz.q: What is the effect of planting onions too close together?
quiz.explanation: Overcrowding causes competition for resources, resulting in smaller bulbs.

quiz.q: What day length do short-day onion varieties require for bulbing?
quiz.explanation: Short-day onions bulb when daylight is 10-12 hours, which is common near the equator.

quiz.q: In tropical Africa, when is the best time to plant short-day onions?
options: B) Start of cool dry season
quiz.explanation: Planting at the start of the cool dry season avoids extreme heat and allows proper bulbing.

quiz.q: What happens if onions are planted too late in the season?
options: B) Bulbs may not size up properly
quiz.explanation: Late planting can result in bulbs forming when days are still long, leading to poor bulb development.

quiz.q: How many days from seed to harvest for onions?
quiz.explanation: Onions take about 100-120 days from seed to harvest, depending on variety and conditions.

quiz.q: What is the ideal soil temperature for onion seed germination?
quiz.explanation: Onion seeds germinate best when soil temperature is between 15-25Â°C.

quiz.q: Why is crop rotation important for onions?
options: B) To prevent pest and disease buildup
quiz.explanation: Rotating crops prevents soil-borne pests and diseases specific to onions from accumulating.

quiz.q: What is the recommended spacing for green onions?
quiz.explanation: Green onions can be planted closer, at 5-7 cm between plants and 15-20 cm between rows.

quiz.q: What tool is used to make holes for transplanting?
quiz.explanation: A dibber is a pointed stick used to make holes for transplanting seedlings.

quiz.q: What should you do immediately after transplanting?
quiz.explanation: Watering immediately after transplanting settles the soil and reduces shock.

quiz.q: How can you reduce transplanting shock?
options: B) Keep roots moist and transplant in late afternoon
quiz.explanation: Transplanting in late afternoon and keeping roots moist minimizes stress on seedlings.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of hardening off seedlings?
options: A) To make them grow faster
B) To toughen them for field conditions
quiz.explanation: Hardening off gradually exposes seedlings to outdoor conditions, making them more resilient.

quiz.q: What is a common problem when using sets for planting?
options: A) They take too long to grow
B) They are more expensive than seed
D) They are hard to plant
quiz.explanation: Sets are more expensive than seed, though they are faster and easier to plant.

quiz.q: What is the recommended depth for planting sets?
quiz.explanation: Sets should be planted 2-3 cm deep, pointed end up.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid planting onions after onions or garlic?
options: A) They deplete the same nutrients
B) They attract the same pests and diseases
quiz.explanation: Onions and garlic share pests and diseases, so rotating prevents buildup in the soil.

quiz.q: What is the benefit of using raised beds for onions?
quiz.explanation: Raised beds improve drainage, which is crucial because onions are sensitive to waterlogging.

quiz.q: What is the critical day length for long-day onion varieties to bulb?
quiz.explanation: Long-day onions require 14-16 hours of daylight to trigger bulbing.
